Layers

Cities, Events and Administrative are in the header: they turn the three kinds of place on and off, both on the map and in the quiz. Territories stay clickable whatever is switched off, so you can always check anything you can see.

Language of place names

English gives the name as it was used at the time, with the present-day name after it where they differ. Japanese gives the imperial-period form, Chinese is in traditional characters, and Korean is in hangul with McCune–Reischauer romanisation. Explanatory notes stay in English throughout.

How much is asked about

Three sets, from the places every student should know to the full list. This sets how many places the quiz asks about and how many names the map will try to fit.

Names are placed so they do not overlap, so at a wide zoom only some of them fit. Zoom in and more appear.

Provincial capitals and the larger cities of Korea, Taiwan, Japan and Southeast Asia, in smaller grey dots. They are context only — the quiz never asks about them.

On the Dec 1942 map the Yellow River is drawn in the course it took after the Chinese army cut the dikes at Huayuankou in June 1938 to slow the Japanese advance, when it left its bed and ran south-east into the Huai and on through Hungtse Lake into the Yangtze above Chinkiang. It stayed there until the breach was closed in 1947.

A dashed perimeter traced from the "War in the Pacific" map in Andrew Gordon, A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa Times to the Present. It shows on the Late 1942 map only. It is the extent of Japanese control and the fighting front at that date, not a maximum: the naval perimeter was widest in July and August 1942, and the area of China under Japanese control was largest in 1944. Out at sea it marks how far the navy reached rather than territory held. Across China it is the inland edge of the shaded occupied zone itself, so the two agree — a perimeter that claimed ground the shading did not would be saying Japanese forces were where the map elsewhere says they were not. The front it generalises was broad, shifting and porous, and the note on the occupied zone says what that means.

About this map

This interactive map is for practising the geography of the Japanese Empire: the home islands, the formal colonies, the occupied territories and puppet states, the neighbouring countries, and the cities, ports and battlefields that recur in the history of modern Japan from Perry's arrival in 1853 to the surrender in 1945.

How to use it

  • 1930 / Dec 1942 — which map you are looking at. In 1930 the colours show whose empire each place belonged to, on the eve of the Manchurian Incident. In December 1942 they show how Japan held what it had taken.
  • Explore — hover over, or tap, any territory or marker to see what it is, what it was called, when it changed hands, and why it matters.
  • Quiz — you are asked to find a place and you click it on the map. Your score and the places you missed are reported at the end.
  • Basic / Intermediate / Advanced — how many places the quiz asks about, and how many names appear on the map. Every territory stays clickable at every level.
  • English / 日本語 / 中文 / 한국어 — which name is shown. English gives the name as it was used at the time, with the present-day name after it where they differ: Mukden (Shenyang), Taihoku (Taipei), Peking (Beijing), Batavia (Jakarta). Japanese gives the imperial-period form — Keijō for Seoul, Shinkyō for Changchun, Shōnantō for Singapore. Chinese is in traditional characters, as the period used them; Korean is in hangul with McCune-Reischauer romanisation. Explanatory notes stay in English throughout, as do the names of the provinces of Siam and the Philippines, which is how the period's own maps of them are lettered.

A caution about borders

Inside China the boundaries are the real provinces of 1928–45, so Manchukuo is Liaoning, Jilin, Heilongjiang and Jehol as they actually stood, and Mengchiang is Chahar and Suiyuan. Karafuto is Sakhalin south of the 50th parallel, which is where the border ran, and the Kwantung Leased Territory is cut across the Liaodong isthmus on the line of the 1898 lease. Elsewhere, modern coastlines and outlines stand in for historical ones — fine for coasts, rough for land borders.

The area of occupied China is traced from a period map of the occupation rather than drawn as whole provinces, and adjusted to December 1942: the front runs down the Tatung–Puchow railway in Shansi to the Yellow River bend, along the river's north bank — so Loyang and Chengchow are outside it, both holding until 1944 — then down the flood course the river took after Huayuankou, round the Chinese pocket in north-west Anhui and the Dabie Shan, out to Ichang, past Yochow, and through Chekiang taking in Kinhwa but not Chuchow or Wenchow. It is still approximate, and it is still generous: Japanese control ran along the railways and around the cities, and much of the countryside inside the line was held by Communist and Nationalist guerrillas.

Hovering names the sub-unit under the pointer as well as the country: the province, prefecture, residency, state, division or island. These are the units of the period and they carry their period names — Kankyōhoku-dō rather than North Hamgyŏng, Tayabas rather than Quezon, Chiengmai rather than Chiang Mai, Celebes rather than Sulawesi. Their outlines, though, are assembled from modern ones — Korea excepted — so where a boundary has moved since, the shape is an approximation and the name is the thing to trust. Three places to keep in mind. Manchukuo redrew the three north-eastern provinces into nineteen of its own between 1934 and 1941; they are drawn here as Fengtien, Kirin and Heilungkiang, the provinces Manchukuo was made out of. British India's provinces were interleaved with several hundred princely states, which are drawn from a layer of their 1931 boundaries rather than approximated from modern ones; only the smallest are below the resolution of this map, and those are drawn inside whichever province surrounded them. And Siam's changwat sat inside the monthon, the "circles" abolished in 1933, which are not drawn. Korea is the exception to all of this: its thirteen provinces come from a map of the period rather than from modern units, so Hwanghae is one province and Kaesong is in Keiki-dō, where it belonged.

Where several modern states made up one historical territory they are drawn as a single shape with no boundary between them, because there was none: British India has no line at the Punjab, French Indochina none at the Mekong, Korea none at the 38th parallel. Present-day borders that had not been drawn yet do not appear.

The front line moved constantly between 1931 and 1945, and any single date is a snapshot. For close work, use a proper historical atlas.

Sources and credits

Every dataset this map is drawn from is listed below, with what each was used for, where it came from and under what licence, and a note on what was done to the data. In short: coastlines from Natural Earth, China's provinces the real ones of 1928–45, Korea from a map of the period, the princely states georeferenced from a 1931 atlas, and the occupied zone and the line of control traced from period maps and approximate. The fine coastlines and island names of the Ryukyus, the Bonins and the Marianas are © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL, and load only when you zoom in on them.

Sources in full

Boundaries and coastlines

  • Natural Earth, 1:10m cultural vectors. All coastlines and national outlines outside China, and the base for the frame. Public domain — Natural Earth's terms state the data may be used in any manner, including modifying the content and design, and that no permission is needed.
    github.com/nvkelso/natural-earth-vector
  • ENP-China — Chinese provincial boundaries, 1928–1945. Every Chinese land region. These are the actual provinces of the Nanking decade and the war, not modern ones: Jehol is a province, Suiyuan and Chahar are provinces, and Manchukuo is Fengtien, Kirin and Heilungkiang. CC BY 4.0 — "Provinces 1922–1928 © 2021 by ENP-China Project".
    Elites, Networks and Power in Modern China, Aix-Marseille University.
  • geoBoundaries ADM1 and ADM2. The provinces ceded to Thailand in 1941, the northern Malay states, Burma by division, Kengtung by district, the Indian and Japanese first-level units, and the Indonesian residencies. CC BY 4.0.
    github.com/wmgeolab/geoBoundaries · Runfola, D. et al. (2020), "geoBoundaries: A global database of political administrative boundaries", PLoS ONE 15(4): e0231866.
  • The thirteen provinces of colonial Korea. Korea's province boundaries and its coastline, drawn without simplification because the provinces are the finer source. This is why Hwanghae is one province and Kaesong is in Keiki-dō, where it belonged.
    spatialhistory.net/yale/done/korea.html
  • The princely states of India, 1931. Forty polygons of the states as they stood in 1931, georeferenced by the author of this map from the atlas volume of the Imperial Gazetteer of India, 1931. They replaced five modern Indian states standing in for six hundred princely ones.
    dsal.uchicago.edu/reference/gaz_atlas_1931/
  • Modern East Asia GIS. Tannu Tuva, British Weihaiwei, French Kwangchowan and Nepal, from the author's own QGIS project.
  • OpenStreetMap. The fine coastlines of the Ryukyus, the Bonins, the Volcano Islands, the Izu Islands and the Marianas, and the names of a hundred and seventy islands in them — including every island of the Okinawa, Miyako, Yaeyama and Senkaku groups large enough to draw. These are fetched only when the map is zoomed deep into one of those places, so a reader who never leaves the mainland never downloads them. The island names come from an Overpass query for place=island and place=islet, cached in tools/cache/ so the build does not depend on the network.
    © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database Licence. Map data and any derived database are ODbL; the coastline geometry drawn here is a Produced Work under that licence.
    openstreetmap.org/copyright

Rivers

  • Natural Earth, 1:10m rivers and lake centrelines. The Yangtze and the Yellow River. Public domain. Two hand-drawn tails were needed: Natural Earth's Yangtze centreline stops about 200 km short of the sea, and its Yellow River stops short of the Gulf of Chihli.
  • The 1938–47 course of the Yellow River is redrawn from the channel map at disasterhistory.org (Chris Courtney, after Saito et al. 2000): out of the breach below Chengchow, down the Chia-lu into the Ying, down the Ying into the Huai, and through Hungtse Lake and the Grand Canal into the Yangtze above Chinkiang. For nine years the Yellow River reached the sea through the Yangtze's mouth.
    disasterhistory.org

The occupation and the line of control

  • The occupied zone in China is traced from a period map of the occupation rather than drawn as whole provinces, and adjusted to December 1942. It is an approximation and a generous one: Japanese control ran along the railways and around the cities, and much of the countryside inside the line was held by Communist and Nationalist guerrillas.
  • The dashed line on the Dec 1942 map is the extent of Japanese control and the fighting front at that date, traced from the map captioned "War in the Pacific" in Andrew Gordon, A Modern History of Japan: From Tokugawa Times to the Present (Oxford University Press). Gordon's own legend calls it a greatest extent; it is labelled here for its date instead, because December 1942 is not a maximum — the naval perimeter was widest in July and August, the area of China under Japanese control was largest in 1944, and Kwangchowwan, the northern Malay states and direct rule in Indochina all came later.
  • Saharat Thai Doem — Kengtung and the trans-Salween Shan states — follows the map by Xufanc on Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, taken district by district rather than cut off with a straight line.

What was done to the data

Simplification goes by the size of each ring rather than by one tolerance for a whole country, so a fifty-kilometre island is not flattened by a setting chosen for Luzon. Korea, Kengtung and the princely states are drawn at the full detail of their sources. Where a territory is assembled from sub-units, a whole-country shape is laid beneath them all so that a crack between two neighbours drawn from different files shows the country rather than the sea.

Some boundaries are hand-traced constants rather than data: the occupied zone, the ocean stretches of the line of control, the Kwantung lease across the Liaodong isthmus, the cut at Paotow, Chandernagore, Wake Island, and the estuary tails on both rivers. These are marked as such in tools/build_map.py, where each carries a note saying what it is and why it is drawn by hand.

Names

English gives the name as it was used at the time, with the present-day name after it where they differ: Mukden (Shenyang), Taihoku (Taipei), Peking (Beijing), Batavia (Jakarta). Japanese gives the imperial-period form. Chinese is in traditional characters, as the period used them; Korean is in hangul with McCune–Reischauer romanisation. Each place carries only the scripts that belong to it — hangul on Korea, a Japanese reading on Japan proper, the colonies and the Manchurian group, and neither on places that answered to neither.

The place list is drawn from the timelines of modern Japanese history used in this module, which in turn rest on Andrew Gordon, A Modern History of Japan; Elise K. Tipton, Modern Japan; Brett L. Walker, A Concise History of Japan; Mikiso Hane and Louise G. Perez, Modern Japan; Kenneth Henshall, Historical Dictionary of Japan to 1945; and Jeremy A. Yellen, Japan at War, 1914–1952.
